headlines: Treasury yields rise as march to multiyear highs continues
Trump-Iran Tensions Trigger Fresh Wall Street Selloff
Update: US Equity Indexes Fall as Iran Talks Stall, Fed Governor Points to Higher Rates, Inflation
Senate tees up college sports bill aimed at regulating NIL deals
Fed's Cook says AI demand 'broadening' to increase inflation
Fetterman joins Democrats in warning Mullin, DHS about election interference

cards.hearing: You may hear that tensions with Iran are back in the headlines, and that stocks slipped today along with some worry about oil.
cards.why: When there's conflict overseas, oil can get more expensive to move around the world, and that can eventually show up at the gas pump or in shipping costs on things we buy.
cards.but: But markets have lived through geopolitical flare-ups before, and a rough day tied to overseas tension is not the same as a reason to change a long-term plan.
cards.story: Picture a ship captain who changes the whole voyage every time there's a storm cloud on the horizon. Most of those clouds pass. The captain who stays the course, adjusting sails but not the destination, is the one who actually gets there.
say: We saw this kind of headline before, and the plan held up.
We stay on course. We don't steer the whole ship because of one cloud.

cards.hearing: You may hear that interest rates ticked higher again, and that a Fed official said inflation pressures are broadening because of things like AI-related demand.
cards.why: Higher interest rates can mean a bigger bill on things like a mortgage, a car loan, or a credit card, so when rates move, people feel it in daily life.
cards.but: But rates moving up on one day, even a notable one, doesn't tell us where they'll be next month or next year, and your plan was built to handle rate ups and downs.
cards.story: Think of interest rates like the weather on a long road trip. Some stretches are windy, some are calm. A good driver adjusts speed a bit, but doesn't turn around and go home over one gusty patch.
say: Rates move. Your plan is built with room for that.
We watch it, we don't panic over it.

cards.hearing: You may hear that stocks had a softer day today, closing out the week on a down note across the board.
cards.why: A wobble in stocks can feel unsettling to hear about, especially when it's paired with other headlines in the news.
cards.but: But a soft day, even a noticeably soft one, is part of the normal rhythm of investing, not a signal to abandon a long-term plan.
cards.story: Picture a garden after a windy afternoon. Some leaves get knocked around, a few branches bend. The gardener doesn't dig up the whole yard. They know the roots are what matter, and those didn't move.
say: A rough day doesn't change your roots, meaning your plan.
We let the wind pass. The plan stays planted.
